ChatGPT 說：

對，前面 1～7 的內容比較適合放進 AGENTS.md 作為長期規則，而不是每次處理一章都重新貼給 Codex。

而且你說得對，Chapter 不應該寫死。未來你可能拿這套方法處理 CCNA、AI、軟體架構、哲學書，甚至規格文件，所以我把它改成比較通用的 Source / Unit / Source Note 架構。

其中：

  • Source：原始 Markdown 資料

  • Unit：一個處理單位，可以是一章、節、主題或一份文件

  • Source Note：原本的 Chapter Note

  • Concept：跨內容重複使用的重要觀念

  • Map：知識關聯圖

  • Question：理解與複習問題

下面這份可以直接作為新的 AGENTS.md。

AGENTS.md

1. Purpose

This Obsidian Vault is a structured knowledge base built from source materials such as:

  • Books

  • PDF-to-Markdown documents

  • Technical documentation

  • Research papers

  • Course materials

  • Standards

  • Specifications

  • Notes

The goal is not merely to summarize source material.

The primary goal is to transform linear source material into a reusable knowledge network consisting of:

  1. Source Notes

  2. Concepts

  3. Relationships

  4. Knowledge Maps

  5. Questions

  6. Cross-source connections

The knowledge base should emphasize:

  • prerequisite

  • dependency

  • cause-effect

  • problem-solution

  • leads-to

  • contrast

  • cross-unit relationships

  • cross-source relationships

Codex performs the mechanical extraction and organization.

The user remains responsible for final understanding and validation of important relationships.

2. Vault Structure

Use the following default directory structure:

/
├── 00-Source/
├── 01-Units/
├── 02-Source-Notes/
├── 03-Concepts/
├── 04-Maps/
├── 05-Questions/
└── AGENTS.md

Directory purpose:

00-Source

Original source materials or converted Markdown.

These files are treated as source-of-truth material.

Do not modify them unless explicitly requested.

01-Units

Source material divided into manageable logical units.

A Unit can represent:

  • a book chapter

  • a section

  • a lesson

  • a topic

  • a paper

  • a technical document

  • a specification section

  • another meaningful source segment

Never assume that a Unit is necessarily a chapter.

02-Source-Notes

Structured notes generated from individual Units.

A Source Note explains:

  • what the Unit is trying to teach

  • which concepts matter

  • why those concepts matter

  • how those concepts relate to existing knowledge

A Source Note is not merely a summary.

03-Concepts

Reusable atomic knowledge notes.

Examples:

VLAN.md
STP.md
Routing-Table.md
REST-API.md
Observer-Pattern.md
Stoicism.md

Concept Notes should represent knowledge that can be referenced from multiple Source Notes.

Do not create a Concept Note for every noun or term appearing in the source.

04-Maps

Knowledge Maps and Maps of Content.

Maps organize concepts by relationships rather than by original source order.

Examples:

Ethernet-Knowledge-Map.md
Routing-Knowledge-Map.md
AI-Agent-Architecture-Map.md
Book-Concept-Map.md

05-Questions

Questions used for:

  • understanding

  • review

  • self-testing

  • identifying knowledge gaps

  • cross-concept reasoning

Questions should favor understanding over memorization.

3. Source Protection Rules

Source files are evidence.

Do not modify source material unless explicitly instructed.

Default behavior:

READ source
       ↓
ANALYZE source
       ↓
CREATE / UPDATE notes

Never:

READ source
       ↓
rewrite source file

unless explicitly requested.

Rules:

  1. Do not alter original source wording.

  2. Do not silently correct technical statements in source files.

  3. Do not delete source content.

  4. Do not replace source material with summaries.

  5. Keep AI-generated knowledge separate from original source material.

4. Processing a Unit

When asked to process a Unit, perform the following workflow.

Unit
 ↓
Source Note
 ↓
Concept Extraction
 ↓
Relationship Extraction
 ↓
Concept Notes
 ↓
Knowledge Maps
 ↓
Questions
 ↓
Cross-Unit Connections

Do not stop after generating a summary.

5. Generate a Source Note

For each processed Unit, create or update a corresponding Source Note under:

02-Source-Notes/

Recommended structure:

# <Unit Title>

## Core Question

What problem, question, or subject is this Unit primarily addressing?

## Key Ideas

- ...

## Core Concepts

- [[Concept A]]
- [[Concept B]]
- [[Concept C]]

## Important Definitions

...

## Why These Concepts Exist

...

## Cause and Effect

...

## Prerequisites

...

## Depends On

...

## Leads To

...

## Relationships

...

## Contrast

...

## Cross-Unit Relationships

...

## Important Commands / Examples

...

## Common Confusions

...

## Questions

...

## REVIEW

...

Not every heading must contain content.

Do not invent content simply to fill a section.

6. Concept Extraction

Identify concepts that are important enough to participate in the long-term knowledge base.

A Concept is usually worth creating when one or more of the following are true:

  1. It appears across multiple Units.

  2. Other concepts depend on it.

  3. It is an important prerequisite.

  4. It explains an important mechanism.

  5. It represents an important problem or solution.

  6. It participates in several knowledge relationships.

  7. It is central to understanding the broader subject.

  8. It is likely to be referenced later.

Do NOT automatically create Concept Notes for:

  • every technical term

  • every command

  • every person

  • every product name

  • every minor example

  • every abbreviation

Avoid concept fragmentation.

7. Existing Concept Check

Before creating a Concept Note:

Search:

03-Concepts/

for an equivalent existing concept.

Check:

  • exact name

  • synonyms

  • abbreviations

  • alternate spelling

  • singular/plural forms

  • related terminology

Example:

Spanning Tree Protocol
STP
Spanning-Tree

should normally refer to one Concept Note.

Do not create:

STP.md
Spanning-Tree.md
Spanning-Tree-Protocol.md

for the same concept.

Use one canonical Concept Note.

8. Concept Note Structure

When creating a new Concept Note, use approximately:

# Concept Name

## Definition

Concise explanation of the concept.

## Why It Exists

What problem does this concept solve?

## Prerequisites

- [[Concept]]

## Depends On

- [[Concept]]

## Related Concepts

- [[Concept]]

## Leads To

- [[Concept]]

## Contrast With

- [[Concept]]

## Mechanism

How does it work?

## Appears In

- [[Source Note]]

## Questions

- ...

## REVIEW

- ...

Only include useful sections.

Do not create empty sections simply for template completeness.

9. Concept Relationships

Relationship extraction is more important than summary generation.

When analyzing knowledge, actively search for the following relationship types.

Prerequisite

Concept A should normally be understood before Concept B.

A
↓
B

Example:

[[IPv4 Addressing]]
        ↓
[[Subnetting]]

Depends On

Concept B functionally or logically depends on Concept A.

B --depends on--> A

Leads To

Understanding or introducing Concept A naturally leads to Concept B.

A
↓
B

Cause → Effect

Cause
↓
Effect

Example:

Layer 2 Loop
↓
Broadcast Storm

Problem → Solution

Problem
↓
Technology / Concept

Example:

Layer 2 Loop
↓
[[STP]]

Contrast

Concepts may appear similar but must be distinguished.

Example:

[[VLAN]]
vs
[[Subnet]]

Related

Use related when a stronger semantic relationship cannot be justified.

Do not label every connection as dependency.

10. Relationship Confidence

Do not convert uncertain inference into fact.

Relationships must be separated conceptually into:

Explicit

The relationship is directly supported by source material.

Strongly Inferred

The relationship is technically reasonable and strongly implied.

REVIEW

The relationship may be useful but requires human confirmation.

When uncertain:

## REVIEW

- Possible relationship:
  [[Concept A]] → [[Concept B]]

  Reason:
  ...

  Needs manual verification.

Do not fabricate certainty.

11. Use Obsidian Wikilinks

Use Obsidian wikilinks for established Concepts and Notes.

Example:

[[VLAN]]
[[STP]]
[[Routing Table]]

Prefer links to existing notes.

Do not create links merely to increase Graph View connectivity.

Every link should have semantic value.

12. Update Existing Concepts

When a processed Unit provides additional useful information about an existing Concept:

Update the existing Concept Note when appropriate.

Possible additions:

  • new source reference

  • new prerequisite

  • new relationship

  • new contrast

  • improved explanation

  • important example

  • new question

Do not overwrite good existing explanations unnecessarily.

Preserve useful manually written material.

Prefer additive changes.

13. Generate or Update Knowledge Maps

After concept extraction, inspect:

04-Maps/

Determine whether the Unit contributes to an existing Knowledge Map.

Prefer updating an existing map over creating a duplicate map.

Create a new Map only when the material forms a meaningful reusable knowledge structure.

Maps should emphasize relationships.

Good Map structures include:

Dependency Chain

[[A]]
 ↓
[[B]]
 ↓
[[C]]

Problem → Solution

Problem
 ↓
[[Solution]]

Technology Evolution

Requirement
 ↓
Technology A
 ↓
Limitation
 ↓
Technology B

Hierarchy

Topic
├── [[Concept A]]
├── [[Concept B]]
└── [[Concept C]]

Cause and Effect

Cause
 ↓
Effect
 ↓
Consequence

Troubleshooting Flow

Symptom
 ↓
Check A
 ↓
Check B
 ↓
Root Cause

14. Map Rules

A Knowledge Map is not a duplicate summary.

Maps should help answer:

  • What depends on what?

  • What comes before what?

  • What causes what?

  • Which concepts solve which problems?

  • Which concepts belong together?

  • Which concepts are easily confused?

  • How does one subject lead into another?

Avoid maps that simply reproduce the source table of contents.

15. Generate Questions

For every processed Unit, create or update relevant questions under:

05-Questions/

Question generation should emphasize reasoning.

Preferred question types:

Why

Examples:

  • Why does this technology exist?

  • Why is this mechanism necessary?

  • Why does this behavior occur?

What If

Examples:

  • What happens if this mechanism is removed?

  • What happens if this prerequisite is missing?

  • What happens when this condition changes?

Relationship

Examples:

  • How are A and B related?

  • Why does B depend on A?

  • Why does A lead to B?

Contrast

Examples:

  • What is the difference between A and B?

  • When should A be used instead of B?

  • Why are A and B often confused?

Cause and Effect

Examples:

  • What causes this behavior?

  • What consequences follow from this condition?

Troubleshooting

Examples:

  • If this feature fails, what prerequisite should be checked first?

  • Which symptom suggests failure at this layer?

  • How would you distinguish failure A from failure B?

Cross-Unit

Examples:

  • Which earlier concept is required to understand this?

  • Which later topics depend on this concept?

  • Where else does this concept appear?

16. Avoid Low-Value Questions

Do not make most questions simple definition recall.

Avoid excessive questions such as:

What is VLAN?
What is STP?
What is OSPF?

Prefer:

Why are VLANs needed?

Why does introducing redundant Layer 2 links create a need for STP?

How does VLAN segmentation change the Layer 2 broadcast domain?

Why is a VLAN often associated with an IP subnet even though the two are different concepts?

17. Cross-Unit Relationship Analysis

When processing a Unit, inspect relevant existing:

01-Units/
02-Source-Notes/
03-Concepts/
04-Maps/

Search for relationships including:

  • prerequisite

  • dependency

  • continuation

  • repeated concepts

  • contrast

  • cause-effect

  • shared mechanisms

  • shared protocols

  • problem-solution relationships

Add useful relationships to the Source Note.

Example:

## Cross-Unit Relationships

- [[Ethernet Switching]] provides prerequisites for [[VLAN]].
- [[VLAN]] introduces requirements later used by [[802.1Q]].
- [[STP]] becomes important when redundant Layer 2 paths are introduced.

Do not create artificial relationships solely because two Concepts appear in the same source.

18. Cross-Source Relationships

When multiple books or sources exist in the Vault, concepts should not be isolated by source.

Example:

Book A
   ↓
[[VLAN]]
   ↑
Book B

The Concept Note belongs to the knowledge base, not to a specific book.

Different sources may:

  • reinforce a concept

  • explain it differently

  • provide different examples

  • disagree

  • provide additional detail

Record meaningful differences when useful.

Do not automatically duplicate Concept Notes for each source.

19. Preserve Source Traceability

Important concepts should remain traceable to their source.

Where useful, record:

## Appears In

- [[Source-Note-A]]
- [[Source-Note-B]]

Do not claim that an inference comes directly from a source when it was generated through reasoning.

Maintain a distinction between:

Source statement
vs
AI inference
vs
User understanding

20. Knowledge Consistency

Maintain consistent terminology throughout the Vault.

Before creating a name:

  1. Search existing Concept Notes.

  2. Prefer established terminology.

  3. Use the same capitalization and naming style.

  4. Avoid synonymous duplicate files.

If multiple names are common:

Use one canonical Concept Note and mention aliases inside it.

Example:

# Spanning Tree Protocol

Aliases:

- STP
- Spanning Tree

21. Do Not Over-Link

Links should represent meaningful knowledge relationships.

Bad linking:

Every noun → [[link]]

Good linking:

[[VLAN]]
 ↓ prerequisite / relationship
[[802.1Q]]
 ↓
[[Trunk]]

Graph density is not a goal.

Knowledge clarity is the goal.

22. Do Not Over-Create Concepts

Concept Notes should generally be reusable.

Before creating a Concept, ask:

Will this Concept probably be referenced again?

If no, leave it inside the Source Note unless there is another strong reason to make it standalone.

Prefer:

30 useful Concepts

over:

300 fragmented notes

23. Maps Should Emerge from Concepts

Do not create Maps merely because a Unit was processed.

Create or update a Map when a useful structure has emerged.

Typical signals:

  • three or more related Concepts

  • a clear dependency chain

  • a meaningful cause-effect sequence

  • a technology hierarchy

  • a reusable workflow

  • a troubleshooting structure

  • a cross-source concept cluster

24. Maintain Questions as Knowledge Gaps

Questions are not only quiz material.

They can also represent uncertainty.

Examples:

- Why does this implementation behave differently?
- Is this relationship always true or only under certain conditions?
- Does Source B contradict Source A?

If unresolved, mark them:

REVIEW

Do not force an answer when the sources are insufficient.

25. REVIEW Policy

Use REVIEW whenever:

  • source evidence is weak

  • terminology is ambiguous

  • multiple possible relationships exist

  • a technical inference requires validation

  • two sources appear inconsistent

  • a Concept might duplicate another Concept

  • a Map relationship is uncertain

Example:

## REVIEW

- Determine whether [[A]] truly depends on [[B]]
  or is only commonly associated with it.

Human review is preferred over false certainty.

26. Editing Policy

When modifying generated knowledge files:

Prefer:

preserve
+
extend
+
refine

rather than:

delete
+
rewrite everything

Do not delete manually written material unless explicitly instructed.

Do not replace user explanations merely because another wording is possible.

27. Batch Processing

When multiple Units are processed together:

Do not treat each Unit as an isolated task.

After individual extraction:

  1. Identify repeated Concepts.

  2. Merge duplicate concept candidates.

  3. Identify cross-unit relationships.

  4. Update Maps.

  5. Identify prerequisite chains.

  6. Identify major knowledge hubs.

  7. Generate cross-unit Questions.

  8. Flag inconsistencies.

Example:

Unit A
  ↓
Concept 1
  ↓
Concept 2

Unit B
  ↓
Concept 2
  ↓
Concept 3

Combined knowledge:

Concept 1
   ↓
Concept 2
   ↓
Concept 3

28. Periodic Knowledge Review

After several Units have been processed, perform a higher-level review.

Recommended interval:

3–5 Units

or whenever a major topic group has been completed.

During review, identify:

Knowledge Chains

A → B → C → D

Knowledge Hubs

Concepts referenced by many other Concepts.

Orphan Concepts

Concept Notes with very few meaningful relationships.

Duplicate Concepts

Different files representing essentially the same idea.

Missing Prerequisites

A concept requiring knowledge that is not yet represented.

Missing Maps

Concept clusters that would benefit from a Map.

Knowledge Gaps

Important unanswered questions.

29. Orphan Concept Review

An isolated Concept is not automatically wrong.

However, inspect Concepts that have:

  • no prerequisite

  • no related concepts

  • no incoming references

  • no outgoing relationships

Ask whether:

  1. the Concept should connect to existing knowledge;

  2. the Concept is too minor to deserve a standalone file;

  3. prerequisite knowledge is missing;

  4. the concept is simply genuinely independent.

Do not create arbitrary links just to eliminate orphan nodes.

30. Knowledge Hub Review

Concepts referenced across many Units may represent core knowledge.

When a Knowledge Hub emerges:

Improve that Concept Note.

Consider adding:

  • clearer definition

  • Why It Exists

  • prerequisite chain

  • contrasts

  • examples

  • important relationships

  • relevant Questions

  • dedicated Knowledge Map

Core Concepts deserve more refinement than peripheral Concepts.

31. Source Notes vs Concept Notes

Maintain the distinction:

Source Note

Answers:

What does this part of the source teach?

Concept Note

Answers:

What do I know about this idea across all sources?

Example:

Source Note:
Book-A Unit-05

       ↓ refers to

Concept:
[[VLAN]]

       ↑ also referred to by

Source Note:
Book-B Unit-12

Do not turn Source Notes into duplicate Concept Notes.

32. Maps vs Source Structure

The source structure represents how the author chose to explain material.

Knowledge Maps represent how concepts relate.

These are different.

Example source:

Unit 1
Unit 2
Unit 3
Unit 4

Knowledge Map may instead be:

[[Ethernet]]
     ↓
[[Switching]]
     ↓
[[VLAN]]
     ↓
[[Trunk]]
     ↓
[[STP]]

Do not force knowledge organization to follow source order.

33. Focus on "Why"

Whenever possible, capture:

Why does this exist?

before merely recording:

What is this?

For technical subjects, useful knowledge often follows:

Problem
   ↓
Requirement
   ↓
Concept / Technology
   ↓
Mechanism
   ↓
Limitation
   ↓
Next Concept

This sequence is especially valuable for Knowledge Maps.

34. Focus on Mechanisms

For important Concepts, identify:

Input
 ↓
Mechanism
 ↓
Output

or:

Condition
 ↓
Process
 ↓
Result

Mechanism knowledge is often more reusable than definition memorization.

35. Commands and Examples

Commands, configuration examples, formulas, and code may remain in Source Notes unless they have broader reusable value.

Do not automatically create a Concept Note for every command.

Where appropriate, connect examples to concepts.

Example:

## Important Commands

`show vlan brief`

Related concept:

[[VLAN]]

36. Source Evidence vs General Knowledge

Primary analysis should be grounded in the provided source material.

General technical knowledge may be used to identify possible relationships, but:

  • do not silently mix outside knowledge with source claims;

  • mark uncertain additions as REVIEW;

  • clearly distinguish source-supported statements from inferred relationships when material.

37. Final Processing Report

After processing a Unit or group of Units, provide a concise execution report.

Use:

## Created

- ...

## Updated

- ...

## Reused

- ...

## Relationships Added

- ...

## REVIEW

- ...

Created

List newly created:

  • Source Notes

  • Concept Notes

  • Maps

  • Question files

Updated

List existing files that were modified.

Reused

List existing Concepts reused instead of creating duplicates.

Relationships Added

List important relationships discovered.

REVIEW

List items requiring human validation.

Do not merely respond:

Done.

38. Default Workflow

Unless explicitly instructed otherwise, process a Unit using this order:

1. Read Unit
       ↓
2. Identify core question
       ↓
3. Extract important Concepts
       ↓
4. Search existing Concepts
       ↓
5. Generate Source Note
       ↓
6. Create / update Concept Notes
       ↓
7. Extract relationships
       ↓
8. Build / update Maps
       ↓
9. Generate Questions
       ↓
10. Find cross-unit relationships
       ↓
11. Mark uncertainty as REVIEW
       ↓
12. Produce execution report

39. Core Principle

The goal is NOT:

Source
↓
shorter summary

The goal is:

Source
      ↓
Concepts
      ↓
Relationships
      ↓
Knowledge Network
      ↓
Understanding

Codex should reduce mechanical note-taking work so that the user can spend more time validating, understanding, questioning, and connecting important ideas.

40. Quality Standard

A good processing result should make it easier to answer:

  1. What is this concept?

  2. Why does it exist?

  3. What problem does it solve?

  4. What must I understand before learning it?

  5. What depends on it?

  6. What does it lead to?

  7. What concepts are easily confused with it?

  8. Where else does it appear?

  9. How does it connect to the broader knowledge structure?

  10. What am I still uncertain about?

If the generated notes cannot help answer these questions, improve the knowledge structure rather than generating more text.

之後你實際對 Codex 下的指令就可以縮到很短。例如：

請依照 AGENTS.md 的 Knowledge Extraction Workflow，
處理：

01-Units/05-Network-Time-Protocol.md

請建立或更新：
- Source Note
- Concepts
- Maps
- Questions
- Cross-unit relationships

完成後列出：
Created / Updated / Reused / Relationships Added / REVIEW。

這樣有一個很大的好處：以後不只是 Acing the CCNA Exam 可以用。

例如換成一本 AI 書、哲學書或軟體架構書，AGENTS.md 都不用改，只需要換 01-Units/ 裡的內容。甚至同一個 Obsidian Vault 裡有不同書籍時，03-Concepts/ 還可以逐漸形成真正跨書籍的知識網路。

01-Units 加上條件如下 ：multipule-documents，like 00-Source\Chapter 1, Chapter 2, Chapter 3 ...

ChatGPT 說：

可以。你的意思是 01-Units/ 不一定是一個章節一個來源檔，而是要支援 multiple documents 組成一個 Unit，例如：

00-Source/
├── Chapter 1.md
├── Chapter 2.md
├── Chapter 3.md
├── Chapter 4.md
└── Chapter 5.md

然後 01-Units/ 可以定義：

Unit-01
= Chapter 1 + Chapter 2 + Chapter 3

這很合理，而且比單純「一章 = 一個 Unit」更通用。

我建議把 AGENTS.md 裡關於 01-Units 的定義改成下面這一版。

01-Units

01-Units/ defines the logical processing units used for knowledge extraction.

A Unit does not need to correspond to exactly one source document.

A Unit may contain or reference:

  • one source document

  • multiple source documents

  • multiple chapters

  • multiple sections

  • a selected range of chapters

  • several related technical documents

  • a group of documents covering one logical topic

A Unit is therefore a logical knowledge-processing boundary, not necessarily a physical source file.

Single-Document Unit

Example:

00-Source/
└── Chapter-05.md

A Unit may simply represent:

Unit-05
→ Chapter-05.md

Multiple-Document Unit

A Unit may combine several related source documents.

Example:

00-Source/
├── Chapter-01.md
├── Chapter-02.md
├── Chapter-03.md
├── Chapter-04.md
└── Chapter-05.md

A Unit may be defined as:

Unit-01
├── Chapter-01.md
├── Chapter-02.md
└── Chapter-03.md

This means Codex should treat the three source documents as one logical analysis scope.

The purpose is to identify knowledge that may span document boundaries, including:

  • shared Concepts

  • prerequisite chains

  • repeated terminology

  • cause-effect relationships

  • continuation of an idea

  • cross-document dependencies

  • contradictions

  • concept evolution

Example Unit Definition

A Unit definition may use a Markdown file such as:

01-Units/Unit-01-Network-Fundamentals.md

Example content:

# Unit: Network Fundamentals

## Sources

- [[../00-Source/Chapter-01]]
- [[../00-Source/Chapter-02]]
- [[../00-Source/Chapter-03]]

## Processing Goal

Treat all listed source documents as one logical knowledge unit.

Focus on:

- common Concepts
- prerequisite relationships
- concepts introduced in one document and reused in another
- concepts that evolve across documents
- cross-document dependencies
- important differences or contradictions

Unit Processing Rule

When processing a Unit, first determine all source documents referenced by that Unit.

Processing should conceptually follow:

Unit
 ↓
Resolve Source Documents
 ↓
Read All Relevant Sources
 ↓
Analyze Each Source
 ↓
Analyze Relationships Across Sources
 ↓
Generate Source Note
 ↓
Update Concepts
 ↓
Update Maps
 ↓
Generate Questions

Do not analyze only the first document in a multi-document Unit.

Multi-Document Analysis

When multiple documents belong to one Unit, analyze both:

Within-document relationships

Relationships found inside each individual source document.

Cross-document relationships

Relationships that emerge only when the documents are considered together.

Examples:

Chapter 1
[[Ethernet]]
     ↓
Chapter 2
[[Switching]]
     ↓
Chapter 3
[[VLAN]]

The resulting Unit-level knowledge chain may therefore be:

[[Ethernet]]
     ↓
[[Switching]]
     ↓
[[VLAN]]

even though the complete chain does not appear in a single document.

Concept Reuse Across Documents

When the same Concept appears in several source documents within a Unit:

Do not create separate Concept Notes.

Example:

Chapter-01
   ↓
[[MAC Address]]
   ↑
Chapter-02
   ↑
Chapter-03

Use one canonical Concept Note:

03-Concepts/MAC-Address.md

and record all relevant source references under:

## Appears In

- [[Source-Note-Chapter-01]]
- [[Source-Note-Chapter-02]]
- [[Source-Note-Chapter-03]]

Source Note Strategy for Multiple Documents

For a multi-document Unit, create a Unit-level Source Note under:

02-Source-Notes/

For example:

02-Source-Notes/Unit-01-Network-Fundamentals.md

Recommended structure:

# Unit 01 — Network Fundamentals

## Sources

- [[Chapter-01]]
- [[Chapter-02]]
- [[Chapter-03]]

## Core Question

What larger topic do these documents collectively explain?

## Key Ideas

...

## Core Concepts

...

## Knowledge Progression

[[Concept A]]
↓
[[Concept B]]
↓
[[Concept C]]

## Cross-Document Relationships

...

## Prerequisites

...

## Depends On

...

## Leads To

...

## Contrasts

...

## Questions

...

## REVIEW

...

Optional Per-Document Notes

If detailed per-document notes are useful, Codex may also create individual Source Notes.

Example:

02-Source-Notes/
├── Chapter-01-Note.md
├── Chapter-02-Note.md
├── Chapter-03-Note.md
└── Unit-01-Network-Fundamentals.md

The Unit-level note should focus on the combined knowledge structure and should not simply concatenate the individual notes.

Avoid Duplicate Summaries

For multiple-document Units, do not produce:

Summary of Chapter 1
+
Summary of Chapter 2
+
Summary of Chapter 3

as the main Unit result.

Prefer:

Chapter 1
      ↘
       Concept A
          ↓
       Concept B
          ↓
       Concept C
      ↗
Chapter 3

The purpose of combining documents is to discover knowledge relationships that are not obvious when each source is processed independently.

Overlapping Units

The same source document may belong to more than one Unit when useful.

Example:

Chapter-03.md

may belong to:

Unit-Network-Access

and also:

Unit-Layer2-Troubleshooting

This is allowed because Units represent logical analysis scopes.

Do not duplicate the original source file.

Reuse the same source reference.

Unit Naming

Prefer meaningful topic-based Unit names when possible.

Good:

Unit-Network-Fundamentals
Unit-Layer2-Switching
Unit-Routing-Basics
Unit-Network-Security

Acceptable:

Unit-01
Unit-02

Avoid naming that assumes every Unit equals a single chapter.

Core Rule

A Unit should be interpreted as:

A collection of one or more source documents that should be analyzed together because they form one meaningful knowledge context.

Therefore:

1 Unit
≠
necessarily 1 document

Instead:

1 Unit
=
1 logical knowledge scope
=
1 or multiple source documents

from pathlib import Path

content = r"""# AGENTS.md

## 1. Purpose

This Obsidian Vault is a structured knowledge base built from source materials such as:

- Books
- PDF-to-Markdown documents
- Technical documentation
- Research papers
- Course materials
- Standards
- Specifications
- Notes

The goal is **not merely to summarize source material**.

The primary goal is to transform linear source material into a reusable knowledge network consisting of:

1. Source Notes
2. Concepts
3. Relationships
4. Knowledge Maps
5. Questions
6. Cross-unit connections
7. Cross-source connections

The knowledge base should emphasize:

- prerequisite
- dependency
- cause-effect
- problem-solution
- leads-to
- contrast
- cross-unit relationships
- cross-source relationships

Codex performs the mechanical extraction and organization.

The user remains responsible for final understanding and validation of important relationships.

---

# 2. Vault Structure

Use the following default directory structure:

```text
/
├── 00-Source/
├── 01-Units/
├── 02-Source-Notes/
├── 03-Concepts/
├── 04-Maps/
├── 05-Questions/
└── AGENTS.md

00-Source

Original source materials or converted Markdown.

These files are treated as source-of-truth material.

Do not modify them unless explicitly requested.

Recommended structure when multiple books or source collections exist:

00-Source/
├── Book-A/
│   ├── Chapter-01.md
│   ├── Chapter-02.md
│   └── Chapter-03.md
└── Book-B/
    ├── Chapter-01.md
    └── Chapter-02.md

01-Units

01-Units/ defines the logical processing units used for knowledge extraction.

A Unit is a logical knowledge-processing boundary, not necessarily one physical document.

A Unit may contain or reference:

  • one source document

  • multiple source documents

  • multiple chapters

  • multiple sections

  • a selected range of chapters

  • several related technical documents

  • a group of documents covering one logical topic

Therefore:

1 Unit
≠
necessarily 1 document

Instead:

1 Unit
=
1 logical knowledge scope
=
1 or multiple source documents

Single-document Unit

Example:

00-Source/
└── Chapter-05.md

A Unit may represent:

Unit-05
→ Chapter-05.md

Multiple-document Unit

Example:

00-Source/
├── Chapter-01.md
├── Chapter-02.md
├── Chapter-03.md
├── Chapter-04.md
└── Chapter-05.md

A Unit may be defined as:

Unit-Network-Fundamentals
├── Chapter-01.md
├── Chapter-02.md
└── Chapter-03.md

Codex must treat all referenced documents as one logical analysis scope.

The purpose is to identify knowledge that may span document boundaries, including:

  • shared Concepts

  • prerequisite chains

  • repeated terminology

  • cause-effect relationships

  • continuation of an idea

  • cross-document dependencies

  • contradictions

  • concept evolution

Recommended Unit definition

Example file:

01-Units/Unit-Network-Fundamentals.md

Example content:

Markdown
# Unit: Network Fundamentals

## Sources

- [[../00-Source/Chapter-01]]
- [[../00-Source/Chapter-02]]
- [[../00-Source/Chapter-03]]

## Processing Goal

Treat all listed source documents as one logical knowledge unit.

Focus on:

- common Concepts
- prerequisite relationships
- concepts introduced in one document and reused in another
- concepts that evolve across documents
- cross-document dependencies
- important differences or contradictions

Overlapping Units

The same source document may belong to more than one Unit when useful.

Example:

Chapter-03.md

may belong to:

Unit-Network-Access

and:

Unit-Layer2-Troubleshooting

Do not duplicate the source file. Reuse the same source reference.

Unit naming

Prefer meaningful topic-based names:

Unit-Network-Fundamentals
Unit-Layer2-Switching
Unit-Routing-Basics
Unit-Network-Security

Numeric names such as Unit-01 are acceptable, but do not assume a Unit equals one chapter.

02-Source-Notes

Structured notes generated from Units.

A Source Note explains:

  • what the Unit is trying to teach

  • which concepts matter

  • why those concepts matter

  • how those concepts relate to existing knowledge

A Source Note is not merely a summary.

For a multi-document Unit, create a Unit-level Source Note such as:

02-Source-Notes/Unit-Network-Fundamentals.md

Optional per-document Source Notes may also be created when useful, but the Unit-level note should focus on the combined knowledge structure rather than concatenating summaries.

03-Concepts

Reusable atomic knowledge notes.

Examples:

VLAN.md
STP.md
Routing-Table.md
REST-API.md
Observer-Pattern.md
Stoicism.md

Concept Notes should represent knowledge that can be referenced from multiple Source Notes.

Do not create a Concept Note for every noun or term appearing in the source.

04-Maps

Knowledge Maps and Maps of Content.

Maps organize concepts by relationships rather than by original source order.

Examples:

Ethernet-Knowledge-Map.md
Routing-Knowledge-Map.md
AI-Agent-Architecture-Map.md
Book-Concept-Map.md

05-Questions

Questions used for:

  • understanding

  • review

  • self-testing

  • identifying knowledge gaps

  • cross-concept reasoning

Questions should favor understanding over memorization.

3. Source Protection Rules

Source files are evidence.

Default behavior:

READ source
       ↓
ANALYZE source
       ↓
CREATE / UPDATE notes

Never modify original source files unless explicitly requested.

Rules:

  1. Do not alter original source wording.

  2. Do not silently correct technical statements in source files.

  3. Do not delete source content.

  4. Do not replace source material with summaries.

  5. Keep AI-generated knowledge separate from original source material.

4. Default Unit Processing Workflow

When asked to process a Unit, follow this order:

1. Read Unit definition
       ↓
2. Resolve all referenced source documents
       ↓
3. Read all relevant sources
       ↓
4. Identify the Unit's core question
       ↓
5. Extract important Concepts
       ↓
6. Search existing Concepts
       ↓
7. Generate / update Source Note
       ↓
8. Create / update Concept Notes
       ↓
9. Extract relationships
       ↓
10. Build / update Maps
       ↓
11. Generate Questions
       ↓
12. Find cross-document and cross-unit relationships
       ↓
13. Mark uncertainty as REVIEW
       ↓
14. Produce execution report

For multi-document Units, do not analyze only the first document.

Analyze both:

  • within-document relationships

  • cross-document relationships

5. Generate a Source Note

For each processed Unit, create or update a corresponding Source Note under:

02-Source-Notes/

Recommended structure:

Markdown
# <Unit Title>

## Sources

- [[Source A]]
- [[Source B]]

## Core Question

What problem, question, or subject is this Unit primarily addressing?

## Key Ideas

- ...

## Core Concepts

- [[Concept A]]
- [[Concept B]]
- [[Concept C]]

## Important Definitions

...

## Why These Concepts Exist

...

## Knowledge Progression

[[Concept A]]
↓
[[Concept B]]
↓
[[Concept C]]

## Cause and Effect

...

## Prerequisites

...

## Depends On

...

## Leads To

...

## Relationships

...

## Contrast

...

## Cross-Document Relationships

...

## Cross-Unit Relationships

...

## Important Commands / Examples

...

## Common Confusions

...

## Questions

...

## REVIEW

...

Not every heading must contain content.

Do not invent content simply to fill a section.

For multi-document Units, avoid producing:

Summary of Document 1
+
Summary of Document 2
+
Summary of Document 3

as the main result.

Prefer a combined knowledge structure.

6. Concept Extraction

Identify concepts important enough to participate in the long-term knowledge base.

A Concept is usually worth creating when one or more of the following are true:

  1. It appears across multiple Units or documents.

  2. Other concepts depend on it.

  3. It is an important prerequisite.

  4. It explains an important mechanism.

  5. It represents an important problem or solution.

  6. It participates in several knowledge relationships.

  7. It is central to understanding the broader subject.

  8. It is likely to be referenced later.

Do NOT automatically create Concept Notes for:

  • every technical term

  • every command

  • every person

  • every product name

  • every minor example

  • every abbreviation

Avoid concept fragmentation.

Before creating a Concept, ask:

Will this Concept probably be referenced again?

If no, leave it inside the Source Note unless there is another strong reason to make it standalone.

Prefer:

30 useful Concepts

over:

300 fragmented notes

7. Existing Concept Check

Before creating a Concept Note, search:

03-Concepts/

Check for:

  • exact name

  • synonyms

  • abbreviations

  • alternate spelling

  • singular/plural forms

  • related terminology

Example:

Spanning Tree Protocol
STP
Spanning-Tree

should normally refer to one Concept Note.

Do not create:

STP.md
Spanning-Tree.md
Spanning-Tree-Protocol.md

for the same concept.

Use one canonical Concept Note.

When the same Concept appears in several documents, reuse the same Concept Note and record all relevant source references.

8. Concept Note Structure

When creating a new Concept Note, use approximately:

Markdown
# Concept Name

## Aliases

- ...

## Definition

Concise explanation of the concept.

## Why It Exists

What problem does this concept solve?

## Prerequisites

- [[Concept]]

## Depends On

- [[Concept]]

## Related Concepts

- [[Concept]]

## Leads To

- [[Concept]]

## Contrast With

- [[Concept]]

## Mechanism

How does it work?

## Appears In

- [[Source Note]]

## Questions

- ...

## REVIEW

- ...

Only include useful sections.

Do not create empty sections simply for template completeness.

9. Concept Relationships

Relationship extraction is more important than summary generation.

Actively search for these relationship types.

Prerequisite

Concept A should normally be understood before Concept B.

A
↓
B

Depends On

Concept B functionally or logically depends on Concept A.

B --depends on--> A

Leads To

Understanding or introducing Concept A naturally leads to Concept B.

A
↓
B

Cause → Effect

Cause
↓
Effect

Problem → Solution

Problem
↓
Technology / Concept

Contrast

Concepts may appear similar but must be distinguished.

[[Concept A]]
vs
[[Concept B]]

Related

Use related when a stronger semantic relationship cannot be justified.

Do not label every connection as dependency.

10. Relationship Confidence

Do not convert uncertain inference into fact.

Relationships should conceptually fall into:

Explicit

Directly supported by the source material.

Strongly Inferred

Technically reasonable and strongly implied.

REVIEW

Potentially useful but requires human confirmation.

When uncertain:

Markdown
## REVIEW

- Possible relationship:
  [[Concept A]] → [[Concept B]]

  Reason:
  ...

  Needs manual verification.

Do not fabricate certainty.

11. Use Obsidian Wikilinks

Use Obsidian wikilinks for established Concepts and Notes.

Example:

Markdown
[[VLAN]]
[[STP]]
[[Routing Table]]

Prefer links to existing notes.

Do not create links merely to increase Graph View connectivity.

Every link should have semantic value.

12. Update Existing Concepts

When a processed Unit provides additional useful information about an existing Concept, update the existing Concept Note when appropriate.

Possible additions:

  • new source reference

  • new prerequisite

  • new relationship

  • new contrast

  • improved explanation

  • important example

  • new question

Do not overwrite good existing explanations unnecessarily.

Preserve useful manually written material.

Prefer additive changes.

13. Generate or Update Knowledge Maps

After concept extraction, inspect:

04-Maps/

Determine whether the Unit contributes to an existing Knowledge Map.

Prefer updating an existing map over creating a duplicate map.

Create a new Map only when the material forms a meaningful reusable knowledge structure.

Useful Map forms include:

Dependency Chain

[[A]]
 ↓
[[B]]
 ↓
[[C]]

Problem → Solution

Problem
 ↓
[[Solution]]

Technology Evolution

Requirement
 ↓
Technology A
 ↓
Limitation
 ↓
Technology B

Hierarchy

Topic
├── [[Concept A]]
├── [[Concept B]]
└── [[Concept C]]

Cause and Effect

Cause
 ↓
Effect
 ↓
Consequence

Troubleshooting Flow

Symptom
 ↓
Check A
 ↓
Check B
 ↓
Root Cause

Maps should emerge from concepts.

Do not create Maps merely because a Unit was processed.

Typical signals for creating a Map:

  • three or more related Concepts

  • a clear dependency chain

  • a meaningful cause-effect sequence

  • a technology hierarchy

  • a reusable workflow

  • a troubleshooting structure

  • a cross-source concept cluster

14. Map Rules

A Knowledge Map is not a duplicate summary.

Maps should help answer:

  • What depends on what?

  • What comes before what?

  • What causes what?

  • Which concepts solve which problems?

  • Which concepts belong together?

  • Which concepts are easily confused?

  • How does one subject lead into another?

Avoid maps that simply reproduce the source table of contents.

15. Generate Questions

For every processed Unit, create or update relevant questions under:

05-Questions/

Question generation should emphasize reasoning.

Preferred question types:

Why

  • Why does this technology exist?

  • Why is this mechanism necessary?

  • Why does this behavior occur?

What If

  • What happens if this mechanism is removed?

  • What happens if this prerequisite is missing?

  • What happens when this condition changes?

Relationship

  • How are A and B related?

  • Why does B depend on A?

  • Why does A lead to B?

Contrast

  • What is the difference between A and B?

  • When should A be used instead of B?

  • Why are A and B often confused?

Cause and Effect

  • What causes this behavior?

  • What consequences follow from this condition?

Troubleshooting

  • If this feature fails, what prerequisite should be checked first?

  • Which symptom suggests failure at this layer?

  • How would you distinguish failure A from failure B?

Cross-Document / Cross-Unit

  • Which earlier concept is required to understand this?

  • Which later topics depend on this concept?

  • Where else does this concept appear?

  • How does one source extend or contradict another?

Avoid excessive definition-only questions such as:

What is VLAN?
What is STP?
What is OSPF?

Prefer reasoning questions.

16. Cross-Document and Cross-Unit Analysis

When processing a Unit, inspect relevant existing:

01-Units/
02-Source-Notes/
03-Concepts/
04-Maps/

Search for relationships including:

  • prerequisite

  • dependency

  • continuation

  • repeated concepts

  • contrast

  • cause-effect

  • shared mechanisms

  • shared protocols

  • problem-solution relationships

For multi-document Units, explicitly look for relationships that emerge only when several documents are considered together.

Example:

Document 1
[[Ethernet]]
     ↓
Document 2
[[Switching]]
     ↓
Document 3
[[VLAN]]

The resulting Unit-level chain may be:

[[Ethernet]]
     ↓
[[Switching]]
     ↓
[[VLAN]]

even if the complete chain never appears in one document.

Do not create artificial relationships solely because two Concepts appear in the same source.

17. Cross-Source Relationships

When multiple books or sources exist in the Vault, concepts should not be isolated by source.

Example:

Book A
   ↓
[[VLAN]]
   ↑
Book B

The Concept Note belongs to the knowledge base, not to a specific book.

Different sources may:

  • reinforce a concept

  • explain it differently

  • provide different examples

  • disagree

  • provide additional detail

Record meaningful differences when useful.

Do not automatically duplicate Concept Notes for each source.

18. Preserve Source Traceability

Important concepts should remain traceable to their source.

Where useful, record:

Markdown
## Appears In

- [[Source-Note-A]]
- [[Source-Note-B]]

Maintain a distinction between:

Source statement
vs
AI inference
vs
User understanding

Do not claim that an inference comes directly from a source when it was generated through reasoning.

19. Knowledge Consistency

Maintain consistent terminology throughout the Vault.

Before creating a name:

  1. Search existing Concept Notes.

  2. Prefer established terminology.

  3. Use the same capitalization and naming style.

  4. Avoid synonymous duplicate files.

If multiple names are common, use one canonical Concept Note and mention aliases inside it.

20. Do Not Over-Link

Links should represent meaningful knowledge relationships.

Bad linking:

Every noun → [[link]]

Good linking:

[[VLAN]]
 ↓
[[802.1Q]]
 ↓
[[Trunk]]

Graph density is not a goal.

Knowledge clarity is the goal.

21. Questions as Knowledge Gaps

Questions are not only quiz material.

They may also represent uncertainty.

Examples:

Markdown
- Why does this implementation behave differently?
- Is this relationship always true or only under certain conditions?
- Does Source B contradict Source A?

If unresolved, mark them:

REVIEW

Do not force an answer when the sources are insufficient.

22. REVIEW Policy

Use REVIEW whenever:

  • source evidence is weak

  • terminology is ambiguous

  • multiple possible relationships exist

  • a technical inference requires validation

  • two sources appear inconsistent

  • a Concept might duplicate another Concept

  • a Map relationship is uncertain

Example:

Markdown
## REVIEW

- Determine whether [[A]] truly depends on [[B]]
  or is only commonly associated with it.

Human review is preferred over false certainty.

23. Editing Policy

When modifying generated knowledge files, prefer:

preserve
+
extend
+
refine

rather than:

delete
+
rewrite everything

Do not delete manually written material unless explicitly instructed.

Do not replace user explanations merely because another wording is possible.

24. Batch Processing

When multiple Units are processed together:

Do not treat each Unit as an isolated task.

After individual extraction:

  1. Identify repeated Concepts.

  2. Merge duplicate concept candidates.

  3. Identify cross-unit relationships.

  4. Update Maps.

  5. Identify prerequisite chains.

  6. Identify major knowledge hubs.

  7. Generate cross-unit Questions.

  8. Flag inconsistencies.

Example:

Unit A
  ↓
Concept 1
  ↓
Concept 2

Unit B
  ↓
Concept 2
  ↓
Concept 3

Combined knowledge:

Concept 1
   ↓
Concept 2
   ↓
Concept 3

25. Periodic Knowledge Review

After several Units have been processed, perform a higher-level review.

Recommended interval:

3–5 Units

or whenever a major topic group has been completed.

During review, identify:

Knowledge Chains

A → B → C → D

Knowledge Hubs

Concepts referenced by many other Concepts.

Orphan Concepts

Concept Notes with very few meaningful relationships.

Duplicate Concepts

Different files representing essentially the same idea.

Missing Prerequisites

A concept requiring knowledge that is not yet represented.

Missing Maps

Concept clusters that would benefit from a Map.

Knowledge Gaps

Important unanswered questions.

26. Orphan Concept Review

An isolated Concept is not automatically wrong.

However, inspect Concepts that have:

  • no prerequisite

  • no related concepts

  • no incoming references

  • no outgoing relationships

Ask whether:

  1. the Concept should connect to existing knowledge;

  2. the Concept is too minor to deserve a standalone file;

  3. prerequisite knowledge is missing;

  4. the Concept is genuinely independent.

Do not create arbitrary links just to eliminate orphan nodes.

27. Knowledge Hub Review

Concepts referenced across many Units may represent core knowledge.

When a Knowledge Hub emerges, improve that Concept Note.

Consider adding:

  • clearer definition

  • Why It Exists

  • prerequisite chain

  • contrasts

  • examples

  • important relationships

  • relevant Questions

  • dedicated Knowledge Map

Core Concepts deserve more refinement than peripheral Concepts.

28. Source Notes vs Concept Notes

Maintain the distinction:

Source Note

Answers:

What does this Unit or source group teach?

Concept Note

Answers:

What do I know about this idea across all sources?

Example:

Source Note:
Unit-A

       ↓ refers to

Concept:
[[VLAN]]

       ↑ also referred to by

Source Note:
Unit-B

Do not turn Source Notes into duplicate Concept Notes.

29. Maps vs Source Structure

The source structure represents how the author chose to explain material.

Knowledge Maps represent how concepts relate.

These are different.

Example source structure:

Document 1
Document 2
Document 3
Document 4

Knowledge Map may instead be:

[[Ethernet]]
     ↓
[[Switching]]
     ↓
[[VLAN]]
     ↓
[[Trunk]]
     ↓
[[STP]]

Do not force knowledge organization to follow source order.

30. Focus on "Why"

Whenever possible, capture:

Why does this exist?

before merely recording:

What is this?

For technical subjects, useful knowledge often follows:

Problem
   ↓
Requirement
   ↓
Concept / Technology
   ↓
Mechanism
   ↓
Limitation
   ↓
Next Concept

This sequence is especially valuable for Knowledge Maps.

31. Focus on Mechanisms

For important Concepts, identify:

Input
 ↓
Mechanism
 ↓
Output

or:

Condition
 ↓
Process
 ↓
Result

Mechanism knowledge is often more reusable than definition memorization.

32. Commands and Examples

Commands, configuration examples, formulas, and code may remain in Source Notes unless they have broader reusable value.

Do not automatically create a Concept Note for every command.

Where appropriate, connect examples to concepts.

Example:

Markdown
## Important Commands

`show vlan brief`

Related concept:

[[VLAN]]

33. Source Evidence vs General Knowledge

Primary analysis should be grounded in the provided source material.

General technical knowledge may be used to identify possible relationships, but:

  • do not silently mix outside knowledge with source claims;

  • mark uncertain additions as REVIEW;

  • clearly distinguish source-supported statements from inferred relationships when material.

34. Final Processing Report

After processing a Unit or group of Units, provide a concise execution report.

Use:

Markdown
## Created

- ...

## Updated

- ...

## Reused

- ...

## Relationships Added

- ...

## REVIEW

- ...

Created

List newly created:

  • Source Notes

  • Concept Notes

  • Maps

  • Question files

Updated

List existing files that were modified.

Reused

List existing Concepts reused instead of creating duplicates.

Relationships Added

List important relationships discovered.

REVIEW

List items requiring human validation.

Do not merely respond:

Done.

35. Core Principle

The goal is NOT:

Source
↓
shorter summary

The goal is:

Source
      ↓
Units
      ↓
Concepts
      ↓
Relationships
      ↓
Knowledge Network
      ↓
Understanding

Codex should reduce mechanical note-taking work so that the user can spend more time validating, understanding, questioning, and connecting important ideas.

36. Quality Standard

A good processing result should make it easier to answer:

  1. What is this concept?

  2. Why does it exist?

  3. What problem does it solve?

  4. What must I understand before learning it?

  5. What depends on it?

  6. What does it lead to?

  7. What concepts are easily confused with it?

  8. Where else does it appear?

  9. How does it connect to the broader knowledge structure?

  10. What am I still uncertain about?

If the generated notes cannot help answer these questions, improve the knowledge structure rather than generating more text.
"""

path = Path("/mnt/data/AGENTS.md")
path.write_text(content, encoding="utf-8")

print(f"Created: {path}")
print(f"Size: {path.stat().st_size/1024:.1f} KB")
print(f"Lines: {len(content.splitlines())}")

STDOUT/STDERR
Created: /mnt/data/AGENTS.md
Size: 24.2 KB
Lines: 1606

不會太大。整理後的 AGENTS.md 約 24 KB、1606 行，對 Codex 當作專案規則檔是合理的。重點是我已經把前面內容去重，並正式加入：

  • 01-Units 支援 single document / multiple documents

  • Unit 定義成「邏輯知識範圍」，不再等同 Chapter

  • Source Note / Concepts / Maps / Questions

  • Cross-document / Cross-unit relationship

  • Concept 去重

  • REVIEW 機制

  • 每 3–5 Units 的週期性知識整理

  • 原始 Source 保護

  • 最後 Created / Updated / Reused / Relationships / REVIEW 報告

你可以直接把它放在 Obsidian Vault 根目錄：

接下來實際對 Codex 的命令就可以縮成：

請依照 AGENTS.md，
處理：

01-Units/Unit-Network-Fundamentals.md

建立或更新：
- Source Note
- Concepts
- Maps
- Questions
- Cross-document / Cross-unit relationships

完成後列出：
Created / Updated / Reused / Relationships Added / REVIEW。

這樣之後換 CCNA、AI、哲學或其他技術書，都可以繼續沿用同一份 AGENTS.md。

ChatGPT 可能會出錯。請查核重要資訊。
